title: Tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers with temperature-induced self-tightening enable ultrastable neural interface

paper_content.abstract:
Neural interfaces are essential for brain-machine communication and closed-loop
neuromodulation. However, achieving durable interfaces between neural tissue and bioelectronics
remains a key challenge, as conventional electronics do not actively conform to the soft, tortuous
3D architecture of neural tissue. We report a tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fiber that actively
contracts to wrap around neural tissues, forming ultrastable neural-electronic interfaces, and
enabling highly reliable neural stimulation and recording. This fiber is fabricated via wet spinning
from a precursor integrating a thermoresponsive polymer and electroactive materials, and exhibits
an ultralow modulus of 0.16 MPa and a phase transition temperature of 26.7 °C. Upon contact with
rat tissue, the polymer chains undergo a hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic transition, expelling water
and contracting the fiber to conform tightly to the sciatic nerve. This ultrastable biointerface
demonstrates reliable neural stimulation, producing stable hindlimb bending responses, while
sciatic nerve action potential recordings show 99.5% signal retention under successive
stimulations.
paper_content.introduction:
Bioelectronic-tissue interfaces are essential for neuroscience research, clinical therapies, and
neuromodulation1-11. As a crucial branch of neuromodulation, peripheral nerve modulation has
shown significant potential for regulating physiological functions and treating various diseases12,13.
For instance, vagus nerve stimulation has been applied to regulate heart rate, modulate
inflammatory responses, and manage drug-resistant epilepsy14,15. Similarly, stimulation of the
ulnar and sciatic nerves has proven effective in relieving chronic pain and restoring muscle
function16-18. Despite these promising applications, the clinical efficacy of peripheral nerve
modulation critically depends on the quality of the electrode-tissue interface, since instability at
the interface can degrade signal quality, reduce stimulation efficiency, and elevate stimulation
thresholds, ultimately limiting the reliability and therapeutic effectiveness of neuromodulation19-
21. Most therapeutic electrodes are fabricated from rigid materials such as platinum and silicon22,23.
These devices typically require partial penetration into neural tissue, increasing the risk of
inflammation and mechanical damage and thereby posing challenges for long-term therapeutic
efficacy24,25. In contrast, flexible film electrodes based on polymer substrates such as
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or parylene-C, combined with electroactive materials including
gold nanoparticles or polypyrrole (PPy), have emerged as promising alternatives26,27. Owing to
their soft and flexible structure, these electrodes can conform closely to neural tissue, thereby
minimizing implantation-induced damage while maintaining high electrical conductivity.
However, under dynamic physiological conditions, such film electrodes often lose intimate contact
with surrounding tissue, resulting in interfacial gaps and subsequent signal degradation or even
therapeutic failure in clinical applications. To address this limitation, enhancing adhesion at the
electrode-tissue interface has become an effective strategy for ensuring stable and continuous
bioelectronic integration under wet and/or dynamic environments.

Current approaches to improve electrode-tissue interface stability mainly rely on interfacial
adhesion mechanisms that involve physical interactions and covalent bonding28,29. Physical
interactions, including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, electrostatic attraction, and
mechanical interlocking, provide reversible adhesion but only moderate adhesion strength30,31.
Covalent bonding, typically introduced through reactive groups such as amino (–NH ), carboxyl
2
(–COOH), and thiol (–SH) on electrode surfaces, forms irreversible chemical linkages with
tissues32,33. This markedly enhances electrode-tissue interfacial stability, even under dynamic
conditions. However, the irreversible nature of such bonding can hinder device removal and
increase the risk of tissue damage.

To address these limitations, active conformal strategies based on smart actuation have been
developed. Smart polymers play a crucial role in these approaches, as their stimulus-responsive
deformation enables active conformity to soft tissue. For example, shape-memory polymer thin-
film electrodes achieve conformal tissue contact through thermally triggered shape recovery of a
deformable polymer substrate carrying metal nanofilm electrodes34. Electrochemically actuated
PPy-based electrodes regulate electrode-tissue contact through voltage-induced redox reactions
that cause reversible expansion and contraction27. Similarly, water-responsive polymer electrodes
based on oriented semicrystalline poly(ethylene oxide) undergo rapid contraction upon exposure
to tissue fluids, enabling tight tissue wrapping through hydration-induced recoiling of amorphous
polymer chains35. Despite these advances, most existing designs still rely on externally applied
stimuli to achieve conformal adaptation. Moreover, film-type electronic devices often struggle to
interface effectively with the intricate, small-scale structures of neural tissues due to geometric
mismatch. Therefore, it is critical to develop advanced bioelectronic devices that can actively adapt
to the complex geometry of small neural tissues through endogenous stimuli, enabling more stable
and efficient signal transmission.

Here, we report a tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fiber that undergoes thermo-triggered contraction
driven by endogenous tissue temperature, allowing the formation of stable biointerfaces. When
interfaced with living tissue, the fiber responds to intrinsic temperature by undergoing a phase
transition, resulting in autonomous contraction and self-tightening without external actuation. The
bioelectronic fiber is designed as a composite hydrogel system integrating a thermoresponsive
poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) matrix, polypyrrole-modified carboxylated multi-walled
carbon nanotubes (PPy@CNT), and biocompatible sodium alginate (SA), fabricated via a scalable
wet-spinning process. The resulting PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT (PSPC) fibers possess mixed ionic-
electronic conductivity while maintaining mechanical compliance with soft tissues. Owing to its
one-dimensional microscale geometry and thermo-adaptive behavior, the bioelectronic fiber
enables stable and adaptive interfacing with soft and curved tissues. We further demonstrate its
potential for reliable neural interfacing in vivo, highlighting bioelectronic fibers as a promising
platform for constructing stable electrode-tissue interfaces.
paper_content.results:
Fabrication and characterization of tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers
The tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers exhibit pronounced thermo-adaptive contraction, leading
to autonomous tightening around surrounding tissues. This contraction behavior is functionally
analogous to the active tightening of a snake coiling around its prey, resulting in stable interface
(Figs. 1a, b). To evaluate this self-tightening and conformal behavior across tissues with different
geometries and curvatures, the sciatic nerve, kidney, skeletal muscle, and heart of rats were
selected. In all cases, the tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers formed stable conformal contact with
these tissue surfaces (Fig. 1c).

To fabricate bioelectronic fibers, the spinning solution consisting of PNIPAm, SA, and
polypyrrole-modified carboxylated multi-walled carbon nanotubes (PPy@CNT), was extruded
into an aqueous Ca2+-based coagulation bath (Fig. 2a)36,37. The synthesis and characterization of
the individual components are detailed as follows. PNIPAm was selected as the temperature-
sensitive polymer owing to its good biocompatibility and a phase transition temperature of ~ 32 °C
close to physiological temperature38,39. PNIPAm was synthesized via free-radical polymerization
of NIPAm in aqueous solution and subsequently purified by dialysis, yielding a polymer with a
molecular weight of ~ 4.9×105 g/mol and a dispersity of 2.3 (Supplementary Fig. 1). PPy@CNT
was obtained through Fe3+-catalyzed in situ polymerization of pyrrole on carboxylated carbon
nanotubes. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed a coating layer on the CNT
surface, suggesting successful PPy deposition (Supplementary Fig. 2). By tuning the concentration
of pyrrole monomers, PPy@CNT composites with different PPy loadings were obtained. The
samples were denoted as PPy @CNT , where x and y represent the mass ratio of PPy to CNT,
x y
respectively. Details are provided in the Methods section. The Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR)
spectra showed that the C-O stretching band of -COOH groups in CNT at 1168 cm−1 became
indistinct in PPy@CNT. Meanwhile, the characteristic absorption peaks of PPy (1459, 1307, and
1045 cm−1) exhibited a blue shift compared with those of pure PPy and CNT, indicating interfacial
interactions between CNT and PPy (Supplementary Fig. 3). The obtained PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT
(PSPC) fiber exhibited reversible volume changes, with pronounced shrinkage observed above its
volume phase transition temperature (VPTT) (Fig. 2b). The fiber contracted at elevated
temperatures and recovered upon cooling, due to the thermally induced collapse of the polymer
network.

The morphology and mechanical properties of the PSPC fiber were further characterized. The dried
fiber showed a diameter of approximately ~345 μm. SEM images revealed a smooth surface and
a crack-free cross-section (Figs. 2c-f). The elongation at break and Young's modulus of the PSPC
fiber were 168% and 160 kPa, respectively, compared with 91% and 60 kPa for PNIPAm/SA (PS)
fibers (Supplementary Fig. 4). This increase in mechanical properties is associated with hydrogen
bond interactions between PPy@CNT and the polymer matrix40,41. To verify these interactions,
FTIR analysis was performed. Compared with PS, the -OH stretching band in PSPC shifted from
3438 to 3424 cm−1, and the C=O stretching band shifted from 1650 to 1629 cm−1, suggesting
enhanced hydrogen-bonding interactions between PPy@CNT and the PNIPAm-SA composite
(Supplementary Fig. 5). The Young's modulus of the PSPC fiber was ~160 kPa, smaller than that
of rat sciatic nerve tissue ~580 kPa42, which may facilitate better mechanical compliance and
highlight its potential for neural applications. To evaluate the structural integrity of PSPC fibers
under physiologically relevant conditions, immersion tests were conducted in PBS at 37 °C for up
to 12 h. Only minor changes in mass and diameter were observed over time, indicating stable fiber
structure (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Thermoresponsive properties and finite element analysis
The thermoresponsive behavior of PSPC fibers was first evaluated to examine their potential for
temperature-induced self-adaptive conformability to neural tissues. Differential scanning
calorimetry (DSC) was performed from 10 to 50 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The endothermic
peak observed in the DSC curve corresponds to the phase transition of the polymer network.
PNIPAm aqueous solutions are widely reported to exhibit a phase transition at ~32 °C43. In contrast,
as shown in Fig. 3a, the phase transition temperature of PS fibers decreased to 23.5 °C, consistent
with the salt-induced reduction in transition temperature44,45. This shift is likely caused by
interactions between Ca2+ and the amide oxygen atoms of PNIPAm, which weaken PNIPAm-water
hydrogen bonding and promotes hydrophobic aggregation and chain contraction at lower
temperatures. Incorporation of PPy@CNT partially offset this decrease, raising the transition
temperature to 26.7 °C in PSPC fibers. This increase can be attributed to hydrogen-bonding
interactions between hydrophilic functional groups on PPy@CNT and the PNIPAm/SA matrix,
which enhance water retention within the polymer network. The increased hydration suppresses
PNIPAm chain aggregation, resulting in an upward shift in temperature. Importantly, the transition
temperature of PSPC fibers remained well below physiological temperature, indicating their
suitability for implantable bioelectronic applications. As mentioned above, the PSPC fibers
experience water expulsion and shrinkage when exposed to heat. Therefore, the water loss ratio
and fiber diameter were measured as indicators of its thermo-responsive deformation. Owing to
its low transition temperature of 26.7 °C, the fibers responded quickly when placed in phosphate-
buffered saline (PBS) at 37 °C. Within 30–50 s, the water loss ratio increased from 10% to 20%,
while the diameter decreased from 410 μm to 360 μm (Fig. 3b). This rapid dehydration and
shrinkage indicate the high sensitivity of fiber to physiological temperature. Moreover, the PSPC
fibers showed reversible size changes during repeated heating and cooling. Its diameter decreased
from 450 μm at 25 °C to 350 μm in PBS at 37 °C, and returned to 450 μm upon cooling back to
25 °C (Fig. 3c). These reversible volume changes confirm the thermo-responsive behavior of the
PSPC fibers and demonstrate their stability and reusability under cyclic conditions.

In vitro simulation tests were carried out to evaluate the tissue-adaptive behavior of PSPC fibers.
To mimic the morphology and mechanical properties of sciatic nerve fibers, soft PDMS was used
to prepare fiber-like structures similar to native nerves, with a modulus of ~380 kPa and a diameter
of ~1.3 mm (Supplementary Fig. 7). PSPC and SA/PPy@CNT (SPC) fibers were first wrapped
around PDMS fibers. Due to their softness, both types of fibers could be physically wound onto
the PDMS. The samples were then immersed in PBS at 37 °C to mimic the physiological
conditions. Upon immersion, the SPC fibers began to detach from the PDMS because of weak
physical interactions. In contrast, the PSPC fibers underwent thermally induced contraction,
forming a tighter interface with the PDMS. When the PDMS fibers were shaken in PBS, PSPC
fibers remained firmly attached, whereas nearly half of the SPC fibers detached. Furthermore,
when one end of the fibers was lifted from the solution, the PSPC fibers pulled the PDMS fiber up
together, while the SPC fibers immediately detached (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Movies 1, 2). These
results indicate that the PSPC fibers can self-adaptively tighten around PDMS fibers, forming a
stable and robust interface. To further evaluate their dynamic thermoresponsive behavior, a PSPC
fiber was wrapped around a PDMS fiber and placed in a temperature-controlled chamber at 37 °C.
The fiber completed self-adaptive contraction within 3 s (Supplementary Movie 3). Finite element
analysis showed that the normal stress generated by PSPC fibers during deformation was only ~3
kPa (Fig. 3e), which is below commonly reported thresholds associated with acute nerve
compression injury of ~9 MPa46. In addition, blood flow after PSPC implantation was
systematically evaluated. No statistically significant (P = 0.08) differences were observed
compared with the sham-operated control group, as indicated by the relative blood flow index
derived from laser speckle contrast imaging (Supplementary Fig. 8). These results suggest that
PSPC implantation does not significantly affect local blood flow.

Electrochemical characterization
The electrochemical property of bioelectronic fibers in PBS were tested to assess their reliability
in neural electrical stimulation and recording. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was
carried out under sinusoidal conditions with an amplitude of 5 mV and frequency range of 1 Hz to
100 kHz. The impedance characteristics of PS, PNIPAm/SA/PPy (PSP), and PSPC fibers were
comparatively evaluated. At 1 kHz, PS fibers exhibited a high impedance of 8064 Ω, which
decreased to 4370 Ω after the incorporation of PPy in PSP fibers. A further reduction was observed
for PSPC fibers containing PPy@CNT (Fig. 4a, and Supplementary Fig. 9). Specifically, as the
PPy-to-CNT mass ratio in PSPC fibers increased from 0.3 to 1.2, the impedance gradually
decreased to ~2.0 kΩ at 1 kHz (Supplementary Fig. 10). These results show that CNT incorporation
effectively reduces the impedance of fibers. The stretchability of PSPC fibers initially increased
with increasing PPy-to-CNT mass ratio, followed by a decline at higher ratios (Supplementary Fig.
11). Considering both impedance and mechanical properties, a PPy-to-CNT mass ratio of 0.8 was
identified as the optimal ratio. Unless otherwise specified, PSPC fibers in the following sections
refer to this composition. In addition, PSPC fibers exhibited lower phase angles at low frequencies
compared with PS fibers, indicating a reduced phase delay between current and voltage. This
reduction in phase lag improves the temporal responsiveness of the current, thereby facilitating
rapid charge delivery during neuroelectric stimulation (Fig. 4b). Other nanomaterials, including
silver nanowires (AgNW) and polyaniline (PANI) nanorods, were also used as conductive fillers
to fabricate similar fibers. These fibers exhibited comparable initial impedance. However, the
impedance of the PANI- and AgNW-based fibers increased during immersion in PBS, whereas the
CNT-based fibers remained stable (Supplementary Fig. 12), owing to the higher chemical and
physicochemical stability of CNT.

A higher charge injection capacity (CIC) enables more efficient charge transfer at the electrode-
tissue interface, thereby allowing more effective electrical stimulation. The CIC of PSPC fibers
increased markedly to 10 μC cm⁻2, about 35 times higher than that of PS fibers, which had a CIC
of 0.28 μC cm⁻2 (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 13). In addition, the charge storage capacity (CSC)
of PSPC fibers was 0.84 mC cm⁻2, nearly nine times higher than that of PS fibers, which was
0.093 mC cm⁻2 (Fig. 4d). It also exceeds the 0.65 mC cm-2 observed for PSP fibers, indicating the
important role of CNT in improving the electrochemical performance (Supplementary Fig. 14).
This enhanced CSC can promote signal transmission, ensuring efficient stimulation and reliable
recording. The improved performance results from the synergistic combination of the highly
conductive CNT and the electrochemically active PPy. Notably, the electrochemical performance
under physiological conditions is a critical factor for neural interfacing. The charge storage and
transport characteristics of PSPC fibers remained stable at 37 °C, showing negligible change,
which indicates good suitability for in vivo applications (Supplementary Figs. 15-17).

Electrochemical stability of PSPC fibers at physiological temperature was evaluated by cyclic
voltammetry (CV). Notably, the CV curves obtained during cycling were highly overlapping, and
a 97% CSC retention was observed after 100 cycles, indicating the excellent electrochemical
stability of PSPC fibers (Figs. 4e, f). Moreover, CV curves showed a gradual increase in the
enclosed area as the scan rate increased from 20 to 500 mV s⁻1, indicating an enhanced current
response. This behavior suggests a hybrid capacitive mechanism governed by both surface redox
reactions and ion diffusion processes (Fig. 4g). Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD)
measurements were performed at various current densities within the potential window of –0.5 to
0.5 V to evaluate the charge-discharge behavior of the fibers. All GCD curves showed nearly
symmetrical triangular shapes across different current densities, indicating well-matched charge
and discharge processes and good electrochemical reversibility of the bioelectronic fibers (Fig. 4h).
Furthermore, the electrochemical stability of the bioelectronic fibers was evaluated by soaking
them in PBS at 37 °C for different durations. They exhibited good stability, with only a slight
impedance change observed after 1 h of soaking (Fig. 4i).

Cytocompatibility and in vivo biocompatibility
The cytocompatibility of the bioelectronic fiber was systematically evaluated. PSPC fibers were
cultured with mouse fibroblasts (L929) to assess cell viability, and cytotoxicity was examined
using CCK-8 assays. Live/dead staining showed that the density of viable L929 cells increased
progressively during the culture period, comparable to that of the control group (Fig. 5a).
Consistently, the optical density (OD) values at 450 nm of cell cultures with PSPC fibers also
increased over time, showing no significant difference from the control group (Fig. 5b). In addition,
the survival rates of cells in the PSPC group remained above 90% (Supplementary Fig. 18),
confirming the non-toxicity of PSPC fibers. Likewise, SPC fibers also exhibited good
cytocompatibility after co-culture with L929 cells (Supplementary Figs. 19-21). To assess in vivo
biocompatibility, PSPC fibers were implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region of rats for one
week. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed no apparent inflammatory response around
the implanted fibers compared with the sham controls. Immunofluorescence staining for α-smooth
muscle actin (α-SMA) and cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68) further revealed no significant (P
= 0.82 for α-SMA; P = 0.75 for CD68) inflammatory or foreign body responses around the
implanted fibers, indicating good in vivo biocompatibility (Figs. 5c-e).

In vivo electrical stimulation and electrophysiological recording
Electrical stimulation of the sciatic nerve was performed to evaluate the in vivo stimulation
performance of the bioelectronic fibers. During stimulation, hindlimb muscle contractions
produced mechanical motion that could destabilize the electrode-nerve interface. PSPC fibers were
wound around the sciatic nerve of rats and closely conformed to its highly curved surface owing
to their thermally induced contraction. This self-adaptive behavior formed a stable and intimate
fiber-nerve interface under dynamic conditions. Under electrical stimulation, clear hindlimb
bending was observed (Figs. 6a, b), indicating effective neural activation and motor responses.

To further evaluate the role of the electrode-nerve interface in stimulation effect, SPC fibers, which
lack the self-contraction function but exhibit comparable electrochemical characteristics, were
used as controls (Supplementary Figs. 13, 22-24). SPC and PSPC fibers were wrapped around the
sciatic nerve and subjected to the same stimulation conditions. As shown in Fig. 6c, both types of
fibers exhibited similar stimulation effects, including movement angle and tension force, at the
beginning of stimulation. After multiple stimulations, however, the response induced by SPC fibers
declined markedly, with the movement angle and tension force dropping to 25.5% and 35.2% of
their initial values, respectively. In contrast, PSPC fibers induced stable responses with minimal
variation (Figs. 6d, e). Notably, stable responses were also maintained over a longer period of three
hours and across different stimulation frequencies, with stimulations delivered at one-hour
intervals (Supplementary Fig. 25). Furthermore, the movement angle increased progressively with
higher stimulation currents (Supplementary Fig. 26), indicating effective and controllable
stimulation. These results demonstrate that the self-adaptive PSPC fibers form a stable fiber-nerve
interface that enables effective electrical stimulation.

The bioelectronic fibers were employed to synchronously record compound nerve action potentials
(CNAP) evoked by neural stimulation. The recording system consisted of a recording electrode, a
reference electrode, and a ground electrode, all of which self-adaptively conformed to the sciatic
nerve to form an ultrastable and intimate interface, thereby enabling reliable signal acquisition
(Fig. 6f). The CNAP of sciatic nerve were synchronously recorded in response to pulsed current
stimulation at different amplitudes. With increasing stimulation amplitude, the CNAP signals were
progressively enhanced, indicating that the stable and conformal fiber-nerve interface enables
accurate and reliable neural recording (Fig. 6g). The cycling stability of neural recordings was also
evaluated. As shown in Fig. 6h, the CNAP signals recorded by PSPC fibers remained stable over
1000 consecutive stimulations, retaining 99.5% of the signal intensity (Supplementary Fig. 27).
The corresponding power spectral density remained nearly unchanged, indicating stable interfacial
contact and signal acquisition. The stable interface formed by the self-adaptive bioelectronic fibers
supports reliable neural monitoring under tissue motion.

In addition to forming stable neural interfaces for signal recording, PSPC fibers can also be applied
at muscle interfaces to monitor other bioelectrical signals, such as compound muscle action
potentials (CMAP). To evaluate their recording performance, PSPC fibers were wound around the
extensor digitorum longus muscle (EDL) of rats. A stimulation current was delivered to the sciatic
nerve using commercial needle electrodes, and clear CMAP signals were simultaneously recorded
from the EDL using PSPC fibers (Supplementary Fig. 28a). The PSPC fibers maintained stable
signals with up to 99.8% intensity retention over a 3 h period, owing to the stable electrode-muscle
interface formed by self-contraction. For comparison, SPC fibers without the self-contraction
function were used as control bioelectrodes. Signals recorded with SPC fibers gradually decreased,
with only 34.2% intensity retention (Supplementary Figs. 28b, c).

Preparation of PNIPAm solution
0.5 g of NIPAm was dissolved in 6.0 g of deionized water, followed by the addition of 0.02 g of
KPS (initiator) and 0.015 mL of TEMED (catalyst) and stirred thoroughly to obtain the mixed
solution. Ultrasonication was then performed in an ice bath (< 5 °C) for 30 min and then allowed
to react for 12 h for free radical polymerization (72% yield). A pure PNIPAm solution with a
polymer content of 6% was obtained by dialysis, which ensured the complete removal of residual
monomer.

Preparation of PPy@CNT
CNT (1.0 g) was added to 5 mL of 0.03 M SDBS solution, stirred for 1 h, followed by ultrasonic
dispersion for 3 h. Subsequently, 0.58 g, 1.45 g, and 2.03 g of pyrrole monomer was added to the
dispersion and stirred for 30 min under an ice bath. Polymerization was initiated by the slow
dropwise addition of 1 mL of 5 M FeCl solution using a dropping funnel, and the reaction was
3
maintained under ice-bath conditions for 12 h. After completion, the products were washed with
anhydrous ethanol until colorless and dried under vacuum at 50 °C for 24 h to obtain PPy@CNT
composites with different PPy-to-CNT mass ratios. The PPy content was determined by weighing
the CNT before and after the polymerization of pyrrole. The composite samples were denoted as
PPy @CNT , where x and y represent the mass ratio of PPy to CNT, respectively. PPy
x y
nanoparticles were synthesized by polymerization of pyrrole (140 μL) in 50 mL of 5 M FeCl
3
aqueous solution under an ice bath for 12 h, followed by centrifugation and washing with
anhydrous ethanol.

Preparation of fibers
All fibers were fabricated by injecting the corresponding spinning solutions into a 5 wt% CaCl
2
coagulation bath. The PNIPAm/SA (PS) spinning solution was prepared by mixing 5.0 g of
PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, and 1.0 g of deionized water. For the preparation of
PNIPAm/SA/PPy (PSP) fibers, the spinning solution was obtained by mixing 5.0 g of PNIPAm
aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, 10 mg of PPy, and 1.0 g of deionized water. A PPy@CNT
dispersion was first prepared by dispersing 10 mg of PPy@CNT in 1.0 g of deionized water. Then,
the resulting dispersion was mixed with 0.08 g of SA and 5.0 g of water to obtain the
SA/PPy@CNT (SPC) spinning solution. The PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT (PSPC) spinning solution
was prepared by mixing 5.0 g of PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, and 1.01 g of the
PPy@CNT dispersion. Three spinning solutions (PNIPAm/SA/CNT, PNIPAm/SA/AgNW, and
PNIPAm/SA/PANI) were prepared by mixing of 5.0 g of PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA,
1.0 g of water, and 10 mg of the corresponding conductive material. Each spinning solution was
injected into the coagulation bath using a syringe with a 0.26 mm needle at an injection rate of 0.2
mL/min. Fibers formed rapidly when the spinning solution was injected into the coagulation bath.
After ~ 20 min of gelation, the fibers were collected and rinsed three times with deionized water.

Preparation of stained PDMS fiber
Stained PDMS fibers with a diameter of 1.3 mm were fabricated using a polymer mold by curing
a PDMS prepolymer/curing agent mixture containing yellow dye. The mixture, prepared at a 20:1
mass ratio of base to curing agent, was cured at 100 °C for 3 h, followed by demolding.

Electrochemical property measurement
The electrochemical workstation (CHI660E, Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Co., Ltd., China) was
used to perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (ElS), cyclic voltammetry (CV), charge
injection capacity (CIC) and galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) measurements in a 0.1 M PBS
solution with a standard three-electrode configuration. A 1 cm bioelectronic fiber with a diameter
of approximately 450 μm, containing 2.8 wt% PPy@CNT in the polymer matrix, was immersed
in PBS and placed between sandwiched between two platinum (Pt) electrodes as the working
electrode. An Ag/AgCl served as the reference electrode, and a Pt sheet (1 cm × 1 cm) was used
as the counter electrode. For EIS measurements, a 5 mV amplitude was applied with a frequency
sweep from 100 to 105 Hz. CV tests were conducted in the range of −0.5~0.5 V at scanning speed
of 20–500 mV/s. CIC was measured by applying biphasic pulses of ±0.5 V with a duration of 0.5
ms versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. GCD measurements were conducted between −0.5
and 0.5 V (vs Ag/AgCl) at current densities from 0.1 to 1 mA cm–2.

Characterization
The structure was observed using the cold field emission scanning electron microscope (SU-8010,
Hitachi). Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) spectra were recorded using the Fourier
transform infrared spectrometer (Nicolet iS50, PerkinElmer). The mechanical properties of fibers
were tested by a universal tensile testing machine (UTM2103, Shenzhen Suns technology). The
tension generated during rat hindlimb movement was recorded with a biometric signal acquisition
and analysis system (RM6240E, Chengdu Instrument Factory) with a muscle tension transducer
(JZJ01, Chengdu Instrument Factory). The phase transition temperature of the fibers were obtained
by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC 3500, NETZSCH Instruments). The Molecular weight
of PNIPAm was determined by gel permeation chromatography (Agilent 1260 Infinity Ⅱ, Agilent
Technologies) with N,N-dimethylformamide as solvent at 25 °C.

Stability of PSPC fibers
PSPC fibers were immersed in PBS at 37 °C for differnt times. At each time point, fibers were
removed, blotted dry, and weighed. Fiber diameters were measured at 37 °C by optical microscopy
at multiple positions, and the mean values were calculated.

Blood flow detection
Blood flow was assessed using a 2LD laser speckle imaging system (OMEGAZONE OZ-2,
OMEGAWAVE, Inc.). The CCD camera captured speckle images of blood flow with an acquisition
time of 1 s at a defined blood vessel location on the nerve surface. The laser speckle intensity
scattered by flowing blood corpuscles was visualized as color-coded speckle maps, from which
the relative blood flow index (a.u.) was calculated over a 30 s measurement period. All
measurements were repeated for four independent samples, and the results are presented as mean
± standard deviation.

Cytocompatibility assessment
The L929 was used as the cell model to evaluate the effects of PSPC and SPC fibers on cell
behaviors. The PSPC and SPC fibers were cut into 2 cm segments, sterilized with 75% alcohol for
30 min, and then irradiated with UV light for 1 h. The fibers were washed with PBS before cell
seeding. L929 cells were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin-streptomycin
solution. Then, cells were seeded on the sterilized fibers at the density of approximately 2×104
cells/well and cultured in the a 5% CO incubator at 37 °C. After culturing for 1, 3 and 5 days, the
2
cell viability and proliferation were assessed using the CCK-8 assay. Briefly, the CCK-8 reagent
was added to each well followed by incubation for 1 h. Then, the absorbance of the supernatants
was measured at 450 nm using the microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo FisherScientific,
USA). At the same time, the fibers were stained using propidium iodide and calcein-AM (2 μM,
Beyotime Biotech, China) for 30 min at 37 °C. Lastly, the live/dead cells were observed with the
fluorescence microscope (Ti-s, Nikon, Japan).

Biocompatibility assessment
In vivo biocompatibility was evaluated by assessing the inflammatory and immune response of
dorsal subcutaneous tissue after implantation of PSPC fibers for one week, with a sham-operated
group serving as the control. Each group consisted of four male SD rats (6-8 weeks old). Rats were
anesthetized with 0.8 mL of 10 wt.% chloral hydrate, and a 1-2 cm dorsal incision was made to
create a subcutaneous pocket for implantation of PSPC fibers (~5 mm in length); sham animals
underwent identical procedures without implantation. Incisions were sutured and saline was
injected subcutaneously. After one week, peri-implant and sham tissues were collected, fixed,
paraffin-embedded, sectioned, and subjected to H&E staining. For immunofluorescence, sections
were antigen-retrieved using citrate buffer for α-SMA or EDTA buffer for CD68, incubated with
primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by Cy3-labeled secondary antibodies. Nuclei were
counterstained with DAPI, and images were acquired using a Nikon Eclipse fluorescence
microscope. Image quantification was performed using ImageJ (v1.53k), and statistical analysis
was conducted with Origin 2021.

Stimulation and recording experiment
For sciatic nerve stimulation, CNAP recording, and CMAP recording, four male SD rats (6-8
weeks) were used for each experiment. The SD rats were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection
of chloral hydrate at a dose of 350 mg/kg body weight before surgery. The rats were then fixed on
a stereotaxic apparatus. The hair over the surgical area was shaved, and the skin was incised to
expose the sciatic nerve. PSPC fibers were gently positioned alongside the exposed sciatic nerve
and manually wound around the nerve with fine forceps, forming three to five closely spaced turns.
After self-shrinking to achieve conformal and stable contact with the nerve, cathode-first, charge-
balanced electrical pulses (150 μA, 1–5 Hz) were delivered through PSPC fibers using a
multichannel biosignal acquisition system (RM6240E, Chengdu Instrument Factory). For action
potentials recording, commercial needle electrodes were used for sciatic nerve stimulations (300
μA, 0.5–1 Hz). CNAP and CMAP recordings were performed in separate experiments. CNAP was
recorded from PSPC fibers integrated with the sciatic nerve as described above, whereas CMAP
was recorded from fibers integrated with the EDL using the same procedure. The signals were
acquired with an RM6240E system and analyzed in MATLAB 2024b.

Action potential signal retention analysis
The action potential signal retention ratio was calculated as the ratio of the signal amplitude after
repeated electrical stimulation to that after the initial stimulation. The signal amplitude was
determined as the difference between the maximum positive peak and the minimum negative
trough.

Statistical analysis
All measurements were performed on four independent samples, and data are presented as mean
± SD. Statistical analysis between two groups were conducted using a two-sided Student’s t-test.
Statistical significance was defined as p ≤ 0.05.

Animal experiment protocols
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of
Donghua University (No. DHUEC-NSFC-2023-48).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I have thoroughly evaluated the manuscript entitled “Tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers with temperature-induced self-tightening enable ultrastable neural interface” (Manuscript Number: NCOMMS-25-86621) submitted by Pan et al. Please find below my comments and suggestions for improvement. The manuscript may be considered for publication after the revision.
Comments:
1. It is not evident whether the authors have evaluated the properties of the system in the absence of CNTs. If such a comparison has not been performed, the authors are strongly encouraged to investigate the properties of the fibers without CNTs to clearly demonstrate the contribution of CNT incorporation. Moreover, the authors should clarify whether alternative nanotube (instead of CNTs) can be used in this system or not.
2. The authors should evaluate the stability of the fabricated fibers after immersion in PBS buffer over different time intervals. This will help understand their structural integrity and suitability for potential applications.
3. Figure 3a and Figure 6 (SI) should be merged into a single plot to enable a clearer and more direct comparison. Additionally, the authors are encouraged to use an alternative method to validate the cloud-point temperature (TCP) and strengthen the reliability of the reported results.
4. In general, hydrophilic sodium/calcium alginate enhances water–polymer interactions, which typically leads to an increase in the LCST (or TCP) of thermoresponsive polymers. However, in the present study, the LCST value is reported to decrease. The authors should clearly explain the underlying reason for this deviation and support their explanation with appropriate literature references where similar behavior has been reported.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript of Pan et al. explores the use of PNIPAM as a matrix for tissue-adaptive fibers that exploit the thermoresponsive behavior of PNIPAM to enable self-tightening upon implantation. Overall, this is an elegant approach to implant soft-matter materials with a conductive interface in a reversible and adhesive manner. Additionally, the authors characterize the different aspects of the material, such as tensile strength, thermal, and electronic properties, necessary to support its function. Biocompatibility is also briefly shown. Although the overall approach is attractive, it is not unique; the authors need to clarify the specific novelty over other approaches, such as shape-memory electrodes or water-responsive films. Additionally, some of the claims, such as “ultrastable,” are not well-supported, and the overall discussion should be improved, namely, the obtained results should be placed into the broader context of neural interface materials.
Comment #1: In the introduction, the authors broadly cover the design rationale, highlighting the need for reversible, yet responsive materials to provide neural interfaces. However, the state of the art remains elusive to the reader, and the specific novelty of the presented work remains unclear. How does the authors’ approach differ from shape-memory electrodes (Sci. Adv., 5,eaaw1066(2019), Nat. Mater. 23, 969–976 (2024)) , water-responsive films as self-tightening bioelectronic interfaces (Nature 624, 295–302 (2023))? This needs to be clarified.
Comment #2: The authors assess the biocompatibility in vitro with mouse fibroblast, which shows negligible cytotoxicity. Additionally, the authors interface their materials with the sciatic nerve. While their results show no toxicity in vitro, it is important to note that this does not mean that the material is biocompatible. As mentioned in the introduction, some materials can cause inflammation, and therefore, I recommend that the authors perform histological assessments on the nerves to demonstrate the absence of inflammation and demonstrate the overall safety of the materials.
Comment#3: While the overall concept is elegant, the level of responsiveness remains unclear. In realistic application scenarios, the described shrinkage needs to occur fast, yet, the time scale at which the response takes place is not described. The manuscript would benefit from additional supplementary videos that demonstrate the time scale at which the responsiveness occurs in simulated implantation scenarios.
Comment#4: The authors claim that the reported neural interfaces are ultrastable, yet it remains unclear what is meant by ultrastable. In their report, there are no durability tests that report a durable performance of the material in an applicational setting. The term ultrastable in the context of neural interfaces would ideally imply durable and reproducible responses over the course of hours, or multiple days.
Comment #5: Throughout the manuscript, the characterization of the materials is predominantly reported to control materials of a similar composition to underline the need for the different components of the composite. Yet, the discussion of the results section would strongly benefit from the contextualization of these results versus other systems, such as state of the art hydrogel electrodes. This would enrich the overall discussion and more clearly indicate the overall novelty of the present work.
Comment #6: In several instances, the reporting of the results is incomplete. For the polymer preparation, dispersity and yield are missing, for the tensile strength, I assume the elongation at break are the represented percentages, not the tensile strength. For the animal experiments, it is unclear how many animals were included and what the overall variability of the responses was. These details need to be better represented in the manuscript to ensure the reproducibility and proper reporting of the results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary
The manuscript entitled “Tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers with temperature-induced self-tightening enable ultrastable neural interface” reports the development of thermoresponsive, self-tightening bioelectronic fibers composed of PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT. The authors demonstrate temperature-triggered self-contraction based on the LCST behavior of PNIPAm, enhanced tissue conformity, mechanical compliance, electrochemical performance, cytocompatibility, and in vivo sciatic nerve stimulation and signal recording in rats.
Overall, the concept is intriguing and has potential significance for neural interface technologies. However, several issues hinder the clarity and completeness of the manuscript. In particular, the Introduction and Results sections contain overlapping or misplaced content; the scientific rationale behind demonstrations on organs other than the sciatic nerve is unclear; and safety considerations are insufficiently addressed. These issues collectively indicate the need for substantial revision.
Major Comments
1. Mixing of Introduction and Results Content (Structural Issue)
The Introduction should clearly present the research background, existing challenges, and the position of this study, without including experimental results such as LCST values or mechanical modulus. Several parts of the manuscript inappropriately mix Introduction-like material into the Results section:
- The conceptual illustration in Fig. 1 and demonstrations on various organs should be described in the Results, not the Introduction.
- In the Results subsection “Fabrication and characterization of tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers,” the first paragraph (p.6) and the LCST explanations spanning p.7–8 redundantly repeat Introduction-level content.
- Similarly, the first paragraph of the subsection “In vivo electrical stimulation and neural signal recording” is partly introductory and should be revised to suit the Results section.
In addition, the Introduction should more clearly describe:
- the rationale for using thermoresponsive materials,
- the significance of LCST behavior,
- distinctions from prior literature, and
- the specific challenges this work aims to address.
2. Unclear Significance of Demonstrations on Non-sciatic Tissues
Fig. 1c shows demonstrations of the fiber wrapped around organs such as the kidney, muscle, and heart. While visually striking, their scientific or engineering significance is not adequately explained.
The authors should clarify:
- Why these organs were chosen,
- Whether tightening may pose compression risks,
- Whether such use-cases are realistic in practical applications,
- Whether the demonstrations are conceptual only or linked to envisioned functionalities.
These points should be addressed in the Discussion.
3. Insufficient Consideration of Safety
The manuscript claims that the generated stress of about 3 kPa is not harmful; however, potential risks such as nerve compression, blood flow obstruction, or inflammatory responses are insufficiently discussed. In particular, if the authors wish to claim that the device “enables long-term neural monitoring,” they must support this statement with long-term inflammation data or relevant literature.
4. Inadequate Discussion of Electrode Comparison (Fundamental Control Difference)
SPC lacks PNIPAm and therefore does not exhibit thermoresponsive contraction. As a result, SPC cannot serve as a complete control for PSPC, since PSPC benefits from temperature-induced tightening and enhanced interface stability. The authors should explicitly acknowledge this limitation.
Furthermore, comparison with conventional metal electrodes and recently reported high-performance hydrogel electrodes is insufficient. The manuscript would benefit from situating PSPC performance within the broader context of existing electrode technologies.
5. Reproducibility and Transparency of In Vivo Experiments
(1) Animal number (n) and variability
The number of rats used is not reported. If multiple animals were used, please specify:
- the sample size (n),
- variability in stimulation-induced limb angles,
- variability in AP amplitude retention (e.g., SD).
(2) Use of only 1 Hz in in vivo stimulation
The authors discuss electrode performance based on stimulation data at a single frequency (1 Hz). Because a single frequency is insufficient to assess stability comprehensively, the authors should either:
- provide data across additional frequencies, or
- justify why 1 Hz is representative.
(3) Long-term monitoring claim
Without inflammation assessment or long-term interface stability data, the claim of enabling long-term neural monitoring is overstated. The authors should support this with experimental results or suitable citations.
Minor Comments
1. Clarification of LCST Determination
Please specify how the LCST was defined from the DSC endothermic peak and show correspondence with swelling/shrinking measurements.
2. Terminology Consistency
The manuscript inconsistently uses “PSPC fiber” and “PSPC fibers.” Please unify the terminology.
3. Editing for Clarity
Some expressions in the Introduction and Discussion are verbose or difficult to follow. Careful language editing is recommended.
4. Redundant SEM Images
Fig. 2f appears almost identical to Supplementary Fig. 2b. Consider removing one of them.
5. Significant Figures
The CIC value (p.13, five lines from the bottom) is reported with four significant digits, inconsistent with other parameters. Please unify the notation.
Recommendation
Major Revision
The study presents valuable concepts and results, but significant improvements are required. Reorganization of the manuscript, clarification of scientific rationale, reinforcement of safety considerations, and greater transparency in in vivo methodology will substantially enhance the clarity and impact of this work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript reports a tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fiber that autonomously conforms to rat sciatic nerves at physiological temperature, forming ultrastable neural interfaces for efficient neural stimulation and reliable recording of nerve action potentials. The thermoresponsive polymer and electroactive materials might be useful in developing a tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fiber. While the premise of this study is interesting, I feel that the manuscript suffers from significant issues regarding material characterization, physical interpretation, and experimental rigor.
A primary concern is the characterization of the PPy coating. The amount of PPy on the CNT surface is a governing factor for the composite's performance, yet the authors have not quantified this accurately. Relying solely on changes in fiber diameter is far too indirect to be reliable, and it is entirely unclear how the film thickness was measured. Without precise quantification here, the subsequent discussion rests on shaky ground.
Regarding mechanical properties, the increase in Young's modulus for the PSPC fiber (to 160 kPa) compared to the PS fiber is noted, but the material hardly seems robust. PNIPAm hydrogels are inherently weak and brittle, and the reported values do not suggest a breakthrough in strength. The authors attribute the slight reinforcement to "interactions" between the PPy@CNT and the polymer matrix, but fail to specify the nature of these interactions. Vague assertions about polymer-filler interactions are insufficient without experimental evidence clarifying the mechanism.
The discussion surrounding thermal properties is particularly problematic. The authors report a DSC transition at 26.7 °C as the "LCST" of the solid fiber. This terminology is incorrect; LCST describes a phase separation temperature for a polymer in solution (an equilibrium state), not a thermal event in a solid composite. Furthermore, the explanation that Ca ions lower this temperature by hindering hydrogen bonding is unconvincing. The text also conflates equilibrium thermodynamics with non-equilibrium factors—such as cross-linking density and water permeability—when attempting to explain the shift based on PPy@CNT dispersion. These concepts need to be disentangled.
Finally, the practical application section raises questions about reproducibility. The method for wrapping the fiber around the nerve is not clearly described. While the authors credit thermal contraction for the tight fit, they overlook the role of surface chemistry: at higher temperatures, the polymer becomes hydrophobic, which likely aids adhesion to the tissue by excluding interfacial water. This mechanism should be considered alongside contraction. Most critically, Figure 5 appears to rely on a single experimental run (n=1). Unless the authors can provide statistical data from repeated trials, the reported utility of the device remains anecdotal rather than scientifically proven.
In conclusion, the concept of using a thermoresponsive polymer for temperature-induced self-tightening is indeed an original aspect of this work. However, this novelty does not extend to the other results presented; given the numerous methodological and interpretative flaws outlined above, I do not feel this paper provides sufficient beneficial information to warrant publication in Nature Communications. As a result, this manuscript does not meet the requirements of urgency and novelty that justify its publication in Nature Communications. I feel that this manuscript cannot provide insight into valuable information for developing tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers. I think that this manuscript does not meet the standards of Nature Communications. As a result, I do not recommend for this paper to be published in Nature Communications.

## Abstract

Neural interfaces are essential for brain-machine communication and closed-loop

## Introduction

Bioelectronic-tissue interfaces are essential for neuroscience research, clinical therapies, and
neuromodulation1-11. As a crucial branch of neuromodulation, peripheral nerve modulation has
shown significant potential for regulating physiological functions and treating various diseases12,13.
For instance, vagus nerve stimulation has been applied to regulate heart rate, modulate
inflammatory responses, and manage drug-resistant epilepsy14,15. Similarly, stimulation of the
ulnar and sciatic nerves has proven effective in relieving chronic pain and restoring muscle
function16-18. Despite these promising applications, the clinical efficacy of peripheral nerve
modulation critically depends on the quality of the electrode-tissue interface, since instability at
the interface can degrade signal quality, reduce stimulation efficiency, and elevate stimulation
thresholds, ultimately limiting the reliability and therapeutic effectiveness of neuromodulation19-
21. Most therapeutic electrodes are fabricated from rigid materials such as platinum and silicon22,23.
These devices typically require partial penetration into neural tissue, increasing the risk of
inflammation and mechanical damage and thereby posing challenges for long-term therapeutic
efficacy24,25. In contrast, flexible film electrodes based on polymer substrates such as
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or parylene-C, combined with electroactive materials including
gold nanoparticles or polypyrrole (PPy), have emerged as promising alternatives26,27. Owing to
their soft and flexible structure, these electrodes can conform closely to neural tissue, thereby
minimizing implantation-induced damage while maintaining high electrical conductivity.
However, under dynamic physiological conditions, such film electrodes often lose intimate contact
with surrounding tissue, resulting in interfacial gaps and subsequent signal degradation or even
therapeutic failure in clinical applications. To address this limitation, enhancing adhesion at the
electrode-tissue interface has become an effective strategy for ensuring stable and continuous
bioelectronic integration under wet and/or dynamic environments.

Current approaches to improve electrode-tissue interface stability mainly rely on interfacial
adhesion mechanisms that involve physical interactions and covalent bonding28,29. Physical
interactions, including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, electrostatic attraction, and
mechanical interlocking, provide reversible adhesion but only moderate adhesion strength30,31.
Covalent bonding, typically introduced through reactive groups such as amino (–NH ), carboxyl
2
(–COOH), and thiol (–SH) on electrode surfaces, forms irreversible chemical linkages with
tissues32,33. This markedly enhances electrode-tissue interfacial stability, even under dynamic
conditions. However, the irreversible nature of such bonding can hinder device removal and
increase the risk of tissue damage.

To address these limitations, active conformal strategies based on smart actuation have been
developed. Smart polymers play a crucial role in these approaches, as their stimulus-responsive
deformation enables active conformity to soft tissue. For example, shape-memory polymer thin-
film electrodes achieve conformal tissue contact through thermally triggered shape recovery of a
deformable polymer substrate carrying metal nanofilm electrodes34. Electrochemically actuated
PPy-based electrodes regulate electrode-tissue contact through voltage-induced redox reactions
that cause reversible expansion and contraction27. Similarly, water-responsive polymer electrodes
based on oriented semicrystalline poly(ethylene oxide) undergo rapid contraction upon exposure
to tissue fluids, enabling tight tissue wrapping through hydration-induced recoiling of amorphous
polymer chains35. Despite these advances, most existing designs still rely on externally applied
stimuli to achieve conformal adaptation. Moreover, film-type electronic devices often struggle to
interface effectively with the intricate, small-scale structures of neural tissues due to geometric
mismatch. Therefore, it is critical to develop advanced bioelectronic devices that can actively adapt
to the complex geometry of small neural tissues through endogenous stimuli, enabling more stable
and efficient signal transmission.

Here, we report a tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fiber that undergoes thermo-triggered contraction
driven by endogenous tissue temperature, allowing the formation of stable biointerfaces. When
interfaced with living tissue, the fiber responds to intrinsic temperature by undergoing a phase
transition, resulting in autonomous contraction and self-tightening without external actuation. The
bioelectronic fiber is designed as a composite hydrogel system integrating a thermoresponsive
poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) matrix, polypyrrole-modified carboxylated multi-walled
carbon nanotubes (PPy@CNT), and biocompatible sodium alginate (SA), fabricated via a scalable
wet-spinning process. The resulting PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT (PSPC) fibers possess mixed ionic-
electronic conductivity while maintaining mechanical compliance with soft tissues. Owing to its
one-dimensional microscale geometry and thermo-adaptive behavior, the bioelectronic fiber
enables stable and adaptive interfacing with soft and curved tissues. We further demonstrate its
potential for reliable neural interfacing in vivo, highlighting bioelectronic fibers as a promising
platform for constructing stable electrode-tissue interfaces.

## Results

Fabrication and characterization of tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers
The tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers exhibit pronounced thermo-adaptive contraction, leading
to autonomous tightening around surrounding tissues. This contraction behavior is functionally
analogous to the active tightening of a snake coiling around its prey, resulting in stable interface
(Figs. 1a, b). To evaluate this self-tightening and conformal behavior across tissues with different
geometries and curvatures, the sciatic nerve, kidney, skeletal muscle, and heart of rats were
selected. In all cases, the tissue-adaptive bioelectronic fibers formed stable conformal contact with
these tissue surfaces (Fig. 1c).

To fabricate bioelectronic fibers, the spinning solution consisting of PNIPAm, SA, and
polypyrrole-modified carboxylated multi-walled carbon nanotubes (PPy@CNT), was extruded
into an aqueous Ca2+-based coagulation bath (Fig. 2a)36,37. The synthesis and characterization of
the individual components are detailed as follows. PNIPAm was selected as the temperature-
sensitive polymer owing to its good biocompatibility and a phase transition temperature of ~ 32 °C
close to physiological temperature38,39. PNIPAm was synthesized via free-radical polymerization
of NIPAm in aqueous solution and subsequently purified by dialysis, yielding a polymer with a
molecular weight of ~ 4.9×105 g/mol and a dispersity of 2.3 (Supplementary Fig. 1). PPy@CNT
was obtained through Fe3+-catalyzed in situ polymerization of pyrrole on carboxylated carbon
nanotubes. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed a coating layer on the CNT
surface, suggesting successful PPy deposition (Supplementary Fig. 2). By tuning the concentration
of pyrrole monomers, PPy@CNT composites with different PPy loadings were obtained. The
samples were denoted as PPy @CNT , where x and y represent the mass ratio of PPy to CNT,
x y
respectively. Details are provided in the Methods section. The Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR)
spectra showed that the C-O stretching band of -COOH groups in CNT at 1168 cm−1 became
indistinct in PPy@CNT. Meanwhile, the characteristic absorption peaks of PPy (1459, 1307, and
1045 cm−1) exhibited a blue shift compared with those of pure PPy and CNT, indicating interfacial
interactions between CNT and PPy (Supplementary Fig. 3). The obtained PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT
(PSPC) fiber exhibited reversible volume changes, with pronounced shrinkage observed above its
volume phase transition temperature (VPTT) (Fig. 2b). The fiber contracted at elevated
temperatures and recovered upon cooling, due to the thermally induced collapse of the polymer
network.

The morphology and mechanical properties of the PSPC fiber were further characterized. The dried
fiber showed a diameter of approximately ~345 μm. SEM images revealed a smooth surface and
a crack-free cross-section (Figs. 2c-f). The elongation at break and Young's modulus of the PSPC
fiber were 168% and 160 kPa, respectively, compared with 91% and 60 kPa for PNIPAm/SA (PS)
fibers (Supplementary Fig. 4). This increase in mechanical properties is associated with hydrogen
bond interactions between PPy@CNT and the polymer matrix40,41. To verify these interactions,
FTIR analysis was performed. Compared with PS, the -OH stretching band in PSPC shifted from
3438 to 3424 cm−1, and the C=O stretching band shifted from 1650 to 1629 cm−1, suggesting
enhanced hydrogen-bonding interactions between PPy@CNT and the PNIPAm-SA composite
(Supplementary Fig. 5). The Young's modulus of the PSPC fiber was ~160 kPa, smaller than that
of rat sciatic nerve tissue ~580 kPa42, which may facilitate better mechanical compliance and
highlight its potential for neural applications. To evaluate the structural integrity of PSPC fibers
under physiologically relevant conditions, immersion tests were conducted in PBS at 37 °C for up
to 12 h. Only minor changes in mass and diameter were observed over time, indicating stable fiber
structure (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Thermoresponsive properties and finite element analysis
The thermoresponsive behavior of PSPC fibers was first evaluated to examine their potential for
temperature-induced self-adaptive conformability to neural tissues. Differential scanning
calorimetry (DSC) was performed from 10 to 50 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The endothermic
peak observed in the DSC curve corresponds to the phase transition of the polymer network.
PNIPAm aqueous solutions are widely reported to exhibit a phase transition at ~32 °C43. In contrast,
as shown in Fig. 3a, the phase transition temperature of PS fibers decreased to 23.5 °C, consistent
with the salt-induced reduction in transition temperature44,45. This shift is likely caused by
interactions between Ca2+ and the amide oxygen atoms of PNIPAm, which weaken PNIPAm-water
hydrogen bonding and promotes hydrophobic aggregation and chain contraction at lower
temperatures. Incorporation of PPy@CNT partially offset this decrease, raising the transition
temperature to 26.7 °C in PSPC fibers. This increase can be attributed to hydrogen-bonding
interactions between hydrophilic functional groups on PPy@CNT and the PNIPAm/SA matrix,
which enhance water retention within the polymer network. The increased hydration suppresses
PNIPAm chain aggregation, resulting in an upward shift in temperature. Importantly, the transition
temperature of PSPC fibers remained well below physiological temperature, indicating their
suitability for implantable bioelectronic applications. As mentioned above, the PSPC fibers
experience water expulsion and shrinkage when exposed to heat. Therefore, the water loss ratio
and fiber diameter were measured as indicators of its thermo-responsive deformation. Owing to
its low transition temperature of 26.7 °C, the fibers responded quickly when placed in phosphate-
buffered saline (PBS) at 37 °C. Within 30–50 s, the water loss ratio increased from 10% to 20%,
while the diameter decreased from 410 μm to 360 μm (Fig. 3b). This rapid dehydration and
shrinkage indicate the high sensitivity of fiber to physiological temperature. Moreover, the PSPC
fibers showed reversible size changes during repeated heating and cooling. Its diameter decreased
from 450 μm at 25 °C to 350 μm in PBS at 37 °C, and returned to 450 μm upon cooling back to
25 °C (Fig. 3c). These reversible volume changes confirm the thermo-responsive behavior of the
PSPC fibers and demonstrate their stability and reusability under cyclic conditions.

In vitro simulation tests were carried out to evaluate the tissue-adaptive behavior of PSPC fibers.
To mimic the morphology and mechanical properties of sciatic nerve fibers, soft PDMS was used
to prepare fiber-like structures similar to native nerves, with a modulus of ~380 kPa and a diameter
of ~1.3 mm (Supplementary Fig. 7). PSPC and SA/PPy@CNT (SPC) fibers were first wrapped
around PDMS fibers. Due to their softness, both types of fibers could be physically wound onto
the PDMS. The samples were then immersed in PBS at 37 °C to mimic the physiological
conditions. Upon immersion, the SPC fibers began to detach from the PDMS because of weak
physical interactions. In contrast, the PSPC fibers underwent thermally induced contraction,
forming a tighter interface with the PDMS. When the PDMS fibers were shaken in PBS, PSPC
fibers remained firmly attached, whereas nearly half of the SPC fibers detached. Furthermore,
when one end of the fibers was lifted from the solution, the PSPC fibers pulled the PDMS fiber up
together, while the SPC fibers immediately detached (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Movies 1, 2). These
results indicate that the PSPC fibers can self-adaptively tighten around PDMS fibers, forming a
stable and robust interface. To further evaluate their dynamic thermoresponsive behavior, a PSPC
fiber was wrapped around a PDMS fiber and placed in a temperature-controlled chamber at 37 °C.
The fiber completed self-adaptive contraction within 3 s (Supplementary Movie 3). Finite element
analysis showed that the normal stress generated by PSPC fibers during deformation was only ~3
kPa (Fig. 3e), which is below commonly reported thresholds associated with acute nerve
compression injury of ~9 MPa46. In addition, blood flow after PSPC implantation was
systematically evaluated. No statistically significant (P = 0.08) differences were observed
compared with the sham-operated control group, as indicated by the relative blood flow index
derived from laser speckle contrast imaging (Supplementary Fig. 8). These results suggest that
PSPC implantation does not significantly affect local blood flow.

Electrochemical characterization
The electrochemical property of bioelectronic fibers in PBS were tested to assess their reliability
in neural electrical stimulation and recording. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was
carried out under sinusoidal conditions with an amplitude of 5 mV and frequency range of 1 Hz to
100 kHz. The impedance characteristics of PS, PNIPAm/SA/PPy (PSP), and PSPC fibers were
comparatively evaluated. At 1 kHz, PS fibers exhibited a high impedance of 8064 Ω, which
decreased to 4370 Ω after the incorporation of PPy in PSP fibers. A further reduction was observed
for PSPC fibers containing PPy@CNT (Fig. 4a, and Supplementary Fig. 9). Specifically, as the
PPy-to-CNT mass ratio in PSPC fibers increased from 0.3 to 1.2, the impedance gradually
decreased to ~2.0 kΩ at 1 kHz (Supplementary Fig. 10). These results show that CNT incorporation
effectively reduces the impedance of fibers. The stretchability of PSPC fibers initially increased
with increasing PPy-to-CNT mass ratio, followed by a decline at higher ratios (Supplementary Fig.
11). Considering both impedance and mechanical properties, a PPy-to-CNT mass ratio of 0.8 was
identified as the optimal ratio. Unless otherwise specified, PSPC fibers in the following sections
refer to this composition. In addition, PSPC fibers exhibited lower phase angles at low frequencies
compared with PS fibers, indicating a reduced phase delay between current and voltage. This
reduction in phase lag improves the temporal responsiveness of the current, thereby facilitating
rapid charge delivery during neuroelectric stimulation (Fig. 4b). Other nanomaterials, including
silver nanowires (AgNW) and polyaniline (PANI) nanorods, were also used as conductive fillers
to fabricate similar fibers. These fibers exhibited comparable initial impedance. However, the
impedance of the PANI- and AgNW-based fibers increased during immersion in PBS, whereas the
CNT-based fibers remained stable (Supplementary Fig. 12), owing to the higher chemical and
physicochemical stability of CNT.

A higher charge injection capacity (CIC) enables more efficient charge transfer at the electrode-
tissue interface, thereby allowing more effective electrical stimulation. The CIC of PSPC fibers
increased markedly to 10 μC cm⁻2, about 35 times higher than that of PS fibers, which had a CIC
of 0.28 μC cm⁻2 (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 13). In addition, the charge storage capacity (CSC)
of PSPC fibers was 0.84 mC cm⁻2, nearly nine times higher than that of PS fibers, which was
0.093 mC cm⁻2 (Fig. 4d). It also exceeds the 0.65 mC cm-2 observed for PSP fibers, indicating the
important role of CNT in improving the electrochemical performance (Supplementary Fig. 14).
This enhanced CSC can promote signal transmission, ensuring efficient stimulation and reliable
recording. The improved performance results from the synergistic combination of the highly
conductive CNT and the electrochemically active PPy. Notably, the electrochemical performance
under physiological conditions is a critical factor for neural interfacing. The charge storage and
transport characteristics of PSPC fibers remained stable at 37 °C, showing negligible change,
which indicates good suitability for in vivo applications (Supplementary Figs. 15-17).

Electrochemical stability of PSPC fibers at physiological temperature was evaluated by cyclic
voltammetry (CV). Notably, the CV curves obtained during cycling were highly overlapping, and
a 97% CSC retention was observed after 100 cycles, indicating the excellent electrochemical
stability of PSPC fibers (Figs. 4e, f). Moreover, CV curves showed a gradual increase in the
enclosed area as the scan rate increased from 20 to 500 mV s⁻1, indicating an enhanced current
response. This behavior suggests a hybrid capacitive mechanism governed by both surface redox
reactions and ion diffusion processes (Fig. 4g). Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD)
measurements were performed at various current densities within the potential window of –0.5 to
0.5 V to evaluate the charge-discharge behavior of the fibers. All GCD curves showed nearly
symmetrical triangular shapes across different current densities, indicating well-matched charge
and discharge processes and good electrochemical reversibility of the bioelectronic fibers (Fig. 4h).
Furthermore, the electrochemical stability of the bioelectronic fibers was evaluated by soaking
them in PBS at 37 °C for different durations. They exhibited good stability, with only a slight
impedance change observed after 1 h of soaking (Fig. 4i).

Cytocompatibility and in vivo biocompatibility
The cytocompatibility of the bioelectronic fiber was systematically evaluated. PSPC fibers were
cultured with mouse fibroblasts (L929) to assess cell viability, and cytotoxicity was examined
using CCK-8 assays. Live/dead staining showed that the density of viable L929 cells increased
progressively during the culture period, comparable to that of the control group (Fig. 5a).
Consistently, the optical density (OD) values at 450 nm of cell cultures with PSPC fibers also
increased over time, showing no significant difference from the control group (Fig. 5b). In addition,
the survival rates of cells in the PSPC group remained above 90% (Supplementary Fig. 18),
confirming the non-toxicity of PSPC fibers. Likewise, SPC fibers also exhibited good
cytocompatibility after co-culture with L929 cells (Supplementary Figs. 19-21). To assess in vivo
biocompatibility, PSPC fibers were implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region of rats for one
week. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed no apparent inflammatory response around
the implanted fibers compared with the sham controls. Immunofluorescence staining for α-smooth
muscle actin (α-SMA) and cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68) further revealed no significant (P
= 0.82 for α-SMA; P = 0.75 for CD68) inflammatory or foreign body responses around the
implanted fibers, indicating good in vivo biocompatibility (Figs. 5c-e).

In vivo electrical stimulation and electrophysiological recording
Electrical stimulation of the sciatic nerve was performed to evaluate the in vivo stimulation
performance of the bioelectronic fibers. During stimulation, hindlimb muscle contractions
produced mechanical motion that could destabilize the electrode-nerve interface. PSPC fibers were
wound around the sciatic nerve of rats and closely conformed to its highly curved surface owing
to their thermally induced contraction. This self-adaptive behavior formed a stable and intimate
fiber-nerve interface under dynamic conditions. Under electrical stimulation, clear hindlimb
bending was observed (Figs. 6a, b), indicating effective neural activation and motor responses.

To further evaluate the role of the electrode-nerve interface in stimulation effect, SPC fibers, which
lack the self-contraction function but exhibit comparable electrochemical characteristics, were
used as controls (Supplementary Figs. 13, 22-24). SPC and PSPC fibers were wrapped around the
sciatic nerve and subjected to the same stimulation conditions. As shown in Fig. 6c, both types of
fibers exhibited similar stimulation effects, including movement angle and tension force, at the
beginning of stimulation. After multiple stimulations, however, the response induced by SPC fibers
declined markedly, with the movement angle and tension force dropping to 25.5% and 35.2% of
their initial values, respectively. In contrast, PSPC fibers induced stable responses with minimal
variation (Figs. 6d, e). Notably, stable responses were also maintained over a longer period of three
hours and across different stimulation frequencies, with stimulations delivered at one-hour
intervals (Supplementary Fig. 25). Furthermore, the movement angle increased progressively with
higher stimulation currents (Supplementary Fig. 26), indicating effective and controllable
stimulation. These results demonstrate that the self-adaptive PSPC fibers form a stable fiber-nerve
interface that enables effective electrical stimulation.

The bioelectronic fibers were employed to synchronously record compound nerve action potentials
(CNAP) evoked by neural stimulation. The recording system consisted of a recording electrode, a
reference electrode, and a ground electrode, all of which self-adaptively conformed to the sciatic
nerve to form an ultrastable and intimate interface, thereby enabling reliable signal acquisition
(Fig. 6f). The CNAP of sciatic nerve were synchronously recorded in response to pulsed current
stimulation at different amplitudes. With increasing stimulation amplitude, the CNAP signals were
progressively enhanced, indicating that the stable and conformal fiber-nerve interface enables
accurate and reliable neural recording (Fig. 6g). The cycling stability of neural recordings was also
evaluated. As shown in Fig. 6h, the CNAP signals recorded by PSPC fibers remained stable over
1000 consecutive stimulations, retaining 99.5% of the signal intensity (Supplementary Fig. 27).
The corresponding power spectral density remained nearly unchanged, indicating stable interfacial
contact and signal acquisition. The stable interface formed by the self-adaptive bioelectronic fibers
supports reliable neural monitoring under tissue motion.

In addition to forming stable neural interfaces for signal recording, PSPC fibers can also be applied
at muscle interfaces to monitor other bioelectrical signals, such as compound muscle action
potentials (CMAP). To evaluate their recording performance, PSPC fibers were wound around the
extensor digitorum longus muscle (EDL) of rats. A stimulation current was delivered to the sciatic
nerve using commercial needle electrodes, and clear CMAP signals were simultaneously recorded
from the EDL using PSPC fibers (Supplementary Fig. 28a). The PSPC fibers maintained stable
signals with up to 99.8% intensity retention over a 3 h period, owing to the stable electrode-muscle
interface formed by self-contraction. For comparison, SPC fibers without the self-contraction
function were used as control bioelectrodes. Signals recorded with SPC fibers gradually decreased,
with only 34.2% intensity retention (Supplementary Figs. 28b, c).

Preparation of PNIPAm solution
0.5 g of NIPAm was dissolved in 6.0 g of deionized water, followed by the addition of 0.02 g of
KPS (initiator) and 0.015 mL of TEMED (catalyst) and stirred thoroughly to obtain the mixed
solution. Ultrasonication was then performed in an ice bath (< 5 °C) for 30 min and then allowed
to react for 12 h for free radical polymerization (72% yield). A pure PNIPAm solution with a
polymer content of 6% was obtained by dialysis, which ensured the complete removal of residual
monomer.

Preparation of PPy@CNT
CNT (1.0 g) was added to 5 mL of 0.03 M SDBS solution, stirred for 1 h, followed by ultrasonic
dispersion for 3 h. Subsequently, 0.58 g, 1.45 g, and 2.03 g of pyrrole monomer was added to the
dispersion and stirred for 30 min under an ice bath. Polymerization was initiated by the slow
dropwise addition of 1 mL of 5 M FeCl solution using a dropping funnel, and the reaction was

anhydrous ethanol until colorless and dried under vacuum at 50 °C for 24 h to obtain PPy@CNT
composites with different PPy-to-CNT mass ratios. The PPy content was determined by weighing
the CNT before and after the polymerization of pyrrole. The composite samples were denoted as
PPy @CNT , where x and y represent the mass ratio of PPy to CNT, respectively. PPy
x y

Preparation of fibers
All fibers were fabricated by injecting the corresponding spinning solutions into a 5 wt% CaCl
2

PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, and 1.0 g of deionized water. For the preparation of
PNIPAm/SA/PPy (PSP) fibers, the spinning solution was obtained by mixing 5.0 g of PNIPAm
aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, 10 mg of PPy, and 1.0 g of deionized water. A PPy@CNT
dispersion was first prepared by dispersing 10 mg of PPy@CNT in 1.0 g of deionized water. Then,
the resulting dispersion was mixed with 0.08 g of SA and 5.0 g of water to obtain the
SA/PPy@CNT (SPC) spinning solution. The PNIPAm/SA/PPy@CNT (PSPC) spinning solution
was prepared by mixing 5.0 g of PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA, and 1.01 g of the
PPy@CNT dispersion. Three spinning solutions (PNIPAm/SA/CNT, PNIPAm/SA/AgNW, and
PNIPAm/SA/PANI) were prepared by mixing of 5.0 g of PNIPAm aqueous solution, 0.08 g of SA,
1.0 g of water, and 10 mg of the corresponding conductive material. Each spinning solution was
injected into the coagulation bath using a syringe with a 0.26 mm needle at an injection rate of 0.2
mL/min. Fibers formed rapidly when the spinning solution was injected into the coagulation bath.
After ~ 20 min of gelation, the fibers were collected and rinsed three times with deionized water.

Stained PDMS fibers with a diameter of 1.3 mm were fabricated using a polymer mold by curing

seeding. L929 cells were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin-streptomycin
solution. Then, cells were seeded on the sterilized fibers at the density of approximately 2×104
cells/well and cultured in the a 5% CO incubator at 37 °C. After culturing for 1, 3 and 5 days, the
